name: Grapefruit seed extract
short: Case report: a woman on warfarin had an INR of 7.9 and a minor haematoma after a product sold as grapefruit seed extract. Tested products held synthetic preservatives; 3 held no real extract.
text: A Swedish case report describes a couple on lifelong warfarin treatment who took drops of a grapefruit seed extract product for 3 days; three days later the woman had a minor haematoma under the skin and an INR (a blood-clotting test) of 7.9. Laboratory analysis of three commercial products found the synthetic preservative benzethonium chloride, with glycerol and water, and no authentic grapefruit seed extract in any of them; benzethonium chloride was a potent inhibitor of the drug-metabolising enzymes CYP3A4 and CYP2C9 in the laboratory, and the authors suggest it was responsible for the raised INR. Other laboratory analyses of commercial products labelled as grapefruit seed extract found benzethonium chloride in concentrations from 0.29% to 21.84% and triclosan in two samples, and in an earlier study benzethonium chloride was detected in all five antimicrobially active extracts of six tested, and three extracts also contained triclosan and methyl parabene; those authors concluded that the antimicrobial activity attributed to grapefruit seed extract is merely due to the synthetic preservatives. The evidence of harm is a single case report.
